_doc: T-3645: every "why" a building's floating card folds behind its button (tools/reading_why.mjs), retold for younger readers. Keyed by the note's own words; a note the Details tab shows too is told in the notes file. Only the younger ages are written; no fact enters that the note does not hold, and the build's own talk (record ids, kit names, pixel and camera readings) is left out, so a young reader gets what was read and from where, and what is a guess.

8-10: The old map marks this building '1½'. That means one floor and a half. So we built a room for carriages, with a low loft above it. Most of the loft sits up inside the roof. How tall each part is, is our guess.

The old map marks this building '2', for two floors. A list once said it had one floor, but the map does not agree. So we built a room for carriages with a loft above it, under a steep roof. How tall each part is, is our guess. The map shows no window sticking out of the roof, so we built none.

The old fire map of 1911 marks this house '2½B'. That means two full floors over a basement. The half floor is an attic up in the roof. We did not build it as a real floor. It is the roof space, lit by a window that sticks out of the roof at the front. The back part has two floors under the same roof edge.

The old fire map of 1911 marks the front of this house '2½B'. That means two full floors of brick, with a half floor up in the roof. An earlier try read the back part's mark by mistake and gave the house a flat top. A drawing from 1893 shows the roof's front slope with no window in it. So the half floor is an attic under the roof, not lit from the street. We do not know if a window on another side lit it, so we built none.

The old fire map of 1911 marks this house '2½B'. That means two full floors of brick, with a half floor up in the roof. A window that sticks out of the roof at the front lights it. The house is brick with a stone front, on the corner of 20th Street.
The old fire map of 1911 marks this house '3', for three full floors. The map does not say it has a basement. The raised main floor over a basement is our guess.

The old fire map of 1911 says this house has three floors over a basement. It says stone, with brick at the back. The photo shows smooth cut stone on the front and the south side too. The brick back is the back part of the house.

The old fire map of 1911 marks this front '3B'. That means three full floors over a basement. The house shares a wall with 1706. An old Christmas picture shows it too. Its front stands taller than the top edge of 1706 next door.
The old fire map of 1911 marks this pair of houses '3B'. Both photos show two brick floors over a basement. On top is a steep roof with rooms inside it. That roof holds the third floor.
The old fire map of 1911 marks this pair of houses '3B'. Both photos show two brick floors over a basement. On top is a steep roof with rooms inside it. That roof holds the third floor.

The old fire map of 1911 marks the front part '3B'. It also gives the brick walls' thickness. Those walls are two floors high, so the third floor is in the roof. The map draws lines that show a steep roof with a flat top. That roof holds the third floor. The house next door, 1736, is marked the same way. A photo of it from about 1890 shows that kind of roof. The back part has two floors.
The old fire map of 1911 says this house has three full floors over a basement, just like 1628. It also marks two small parts behind the house. Those parts wait for later work.

The old fire map of 1911 says this house is brick with a stone front. It has three floors over a basement. A museum calls the house covered in pale stone. The photo shows a smooth, light stone front and south side.

The old fire map of 1911 says three floors over a basement, with a part of two floors. A picture from 1888 shows the third floor of the front is up in the roof. A stone gable over the bay lets in light there. So we built two floors under the roof's edge, with the third in the roof. The brick part behind keeps three floors of walls. The picture shows three rows of windows on its south side.

The old fire map of 1911 marks this brick front '4', for four full floors. The map does not say it has a basement. The space under the raised main floor comes from the high steps our plan for the house gives. It is not read from the map. This is the north half of a pair with 1615.

The old fire map of 1911 marks this brick front '4', for four full floors. The map does not say it has a basement. The space under the raised main floor comes from the high steps our plan for the house gives. It is not read from the map. This is the south half of a pair with 1613.

The old fire map of 1911 marks this stone front '4', for four full floors. It has a curved bay. The map does not say it has a basement. The space under the raised main floor comes from the high steps our plan gives. It is not read from the map.

First, the wide curved front. A picture from 1913 shows the wall and roof edge sweeping round from the north corner. The 1911 fire map draws the front bulging out there. We built it as a curve two floors high, with three windows on each floor. Its windows and their heights are our guesses. Second, there is a round tower on the north side, close behind the front.

The roof sticks out a little past the wall. That is just enough for the stone edge under the slate. The picture shows a stone edge, not a deep overhang. We cut it back a bit, so the bay window stands out past the roof's edge.
The main floor stands 1.4 meters above the ground, as we set it at 1619. That is inside our usual range. The drawing shows it about the same height.

The main floor stands 1.85 meters above the ground. We read it off the old drawing, at the top of the steps by the door. That is good to about one part in ten. It is a little higher than we usually start, so it comes from the drawing.

The old map shows a basement, with a raised main floor above it. This house was built as a pair with 1628, so both share one floor height. It sits inside our usual range and fits a whole number of steps.

The main floor stands 2.3 meters above the ground. We read it off an old drawing of Spalding's rebuilt house. It is a raised basement, so its windows are a full floor high at the sidewalk. That is higher than we usually start, so it comes from the drawing.
The roof slopes at 45 degrees. That is the steepest our plan allows. The roof is behind the front gable, and the gable's edges are steeper still.

The roof's front slope is at 45 degrees. That is the steepest our plan allows. In the drawing, the slates rise behind the gable about as steeply as the gable itself. The third floor is up in the roof. The drawing puts the top of the gable about 13.5 meters up and about 4 meters back. A 45 degree roof reaches that spot.

This is a fifth chimney that the house plan does not list. A photo from 1963 shows it rising from the roof between the north tower and the big arch. A photo from about 1923 shows a chimney over the dining room's bay. The dining room has a fireplace, too. We placed it by reading the photo against the windows below, give or take about 2 feet. Its size is like the others'.
Along the front, under the flat roof, runs a wooden edge on carved brackets. The houses 1634 and 1636 have the same. Our rules for this row of houses give it. No paper or picture shows it.

A wooden edge on carved brackets runs under the roof, round all four walls. The houses 1608 and 1612 beside it have the same. An earlier try built 1616 with no brackets. No picture shows its roof edge either way. No iron trim runs along the top, since none is shown.

A wooden edge on carved brackets runs under the roof, round all four walls. The houses 1608, 1612 and 1616 up the row have the same. An earlier try built 1628 with no brackets. No picture shows its roof edge either way. No iron trim runs along the top, since none is shown.

A bronze panel sits on each side of the stone block. An old photo shows the front one, with soldiers leaving the fort. Another shows the east side. A guide book from 1893 says there are four. We did not carve the pictures on them. We made them pale, as the photo from about 1900 shows them. A print from 1893 shows them new and dark. The 1904 scene uses the later, paler look.
A deep roof edge sits over the brackets, about twenty inches out. Boards close it in below. It is one of the sizes our plan allows for this roof's slope.
A deep roof edge sits over the brackets, as on 1628. Boards close it in below. It is a size our plan allows for this roof's slope.
A deep roof edge sits over the brackets. Boards close it in below. It is a size our plan allows for this roof's slope.

The photo shows a deep roof edge on pairs of carved brackets. It runs round the front and the north side. Below it is a plain band. We built the pairs of brackets, sized off the photo. We did not build the panels between them or the carving. In 1904 this edge sits under the tall roof added in 1886.

In the photo, a deep roof edge on pairs of carved brackets runs round the house. Small attic windows sit between them. Its top is about 13.4 meters up. A newspaper gave the same height. We read its paint from how dark it looks in the photo. The edges print nearly black, much darker than the brick walls beside them. The sky was cloudy, so the dark is paint, not shadow.

Both photos show a deep stone edge at the top of the walls. It runs round the front and both sides. Up close, a row of carved stone blocks holds it up. They are single and evenly spaced, not in pairs, as we once thought. We built them in stone, under the roof's edge.

The front photo shows a deep stone edge at the top of the second floor. Up close, a close row of carved stone blocks holds it up. There are dark panels between them, with a flower shape over each. We count twelve across the main front. Each one is about half a meter high. The other photo shows the same row going round the corner.

A walk of flat stones runs straight out from the foot of the porch steps. It goes through the gap between the posts, out to the sidewalk. It is 1.2 meters wide. No picture shows this walk. Its line, width and stones are our guesses. No lawn is laid. The yard's ground is the app's own.

A walk of flat stones runs straight out from the foot of the porch steps to the sidewalk. It is 1.2 meters wide, the same as the walks at 1613, 1615 and 1619. No picture shows this walk. Its line, width and stones are our guesses. No lawn is laid. The yard's ground is the app's own.

A walk of flat stones runs straight out from the foot of the porch steps to the sidewalk. It is 1.2 meters wide. Its stones, width and path are our guesses. No lawn is laid. The yard's ground is the app's own.

This roof has two slopes, and its top line runs along the front. Half of it can not be seen, so the whole roof is our guess. The drawing shows a steep slate slope facing the street. The south wall rises above it in steps, up to a tall chimney. So the slope meets that wall and rises with it. The drawing does not show what is behind the top line. We let the back slope fall to the back wall.

A round tin gutter runs along the roof's edge. It drains into two round pipes on the back wall. Each pipe ends on a flat stone on the ground. The photo shows no pipe on the stone front. It shows none on the south wall, almost to the back. So we put none there. The pipes stand a little in from the back corners, clear of the brackets.

In the old drawing, a heavy roof edge runs round the front, the bay and the side wing. It is all at one height. We built it as a wooden edge on brackets. The wing has the same deep edge in the drawing. An earlier try gave the wing only a thin board. Now the brackets run round the wing's three sides too.

The roof has four low slopes behind the bracketed edge, like 1628's. An earlier try drew it the same way. No paper or picture shows this roof. A house like this, three floors high, could just as well have had a flat roof. We can not build that kind yet.

The roof has four low slopes behind the bracketed edge. An earlier try drew it the same way. No paper or picture shows this roof. A house like this, three floors high, could just as well have had a flat roof. We can not build that kind yet.

The roof has four low slopes behind the bracketed edge. An earlier try drew a flat roof and left the choice for later. No paper or picture shows this roof. A low roof like this was the most common cover on this street's brick houses of the time.

A small landing sits at the door, 1.1 meters deep. That depth is our guess. It puts the foot of the steps under the first fence post in the old drawing. The drawing shows the landing's rail, but not how deep it is.

A photo from before 1880 shows a low roof of four slopes over the main part and the lower part. Its edges rest on brackets. No later picture shows the roof. A small tower stood on it then. Our notes rule that it is not built.
A low roof of four slopes covers the main part. In the photo, its slopes rise from the roof edge to a flat top with a railing. So the roof is cut off flat there.
In the old drawing, a low roof of four slopes rises over the roof edge. Its slopes run back from the front. The flat top and its railing are left for later work.

Both photos show a low iron fence on a stone curb along the street. Its panels have a band of curly shapes under the top rail. Tall square stone posts stand at its gates and at the south corner. The exact pattern of the curls is our guess. The prints show pairs of loops. The fence stands about 9 meters before the front. The gates stand open into the yard.
The photo shows a low iron railing on stone along the walk. It is open at the foot of the steps. The gates are our guess.

The photo shows a low wall of square stones along the street, in front of the lawn. No fence stands on it. It is about half a meter high. We built the gap for the walk where the wall ends. The next wall in the picture belongs to the house next door.

An old drawing from 1874 shows this roof. Its steep slate sides rise straight from the roof edge. Round-topped windows stick out on the north side. Over the north end of the front is a taller top, with its sides curving over. The owner of this project looked at it and said the curved sides bulged like cupcake frosting. So now they are straight, as in the drawing. We kept the roof the same until 1904.

The photo shows a steep slate roof with round-topped windows in its front. It stood from at least the late 1880s to 1911. We do not know when it was first built. The old fire map shows where the roof's bend runs, a little in from the walls.
A stone edge with a row of small blocks runs along the top of the walls. An old drawing shows it on the whole north side and the front. The south side's edge is our guess.

An old photo from 1888 and a later one show a stone edge under the front roof. Plainer edges run along 18th Street and the alley. How deep they are, and how far they stick out, are our guesses. The alley edge starts past the north part, so it no longer sticks out into the air.

The front photo shows a door with panels and a window over it. The house number, 1815, is on it. It sits at the top of steps between stone posts. Over the door is a stone peak on two small carved brackets. A carved knob tops it. We read its size and height off the photo. On the north, the landing runs on past the steps to a stone post. Under it is a dark basement door.

As the old drawing shows, a door with panels sits up a flight of steps. It is between the bay and the side wing. The yard runs about 10 meters to the street. The landing and the steps have a railing of round posts on each side. The drawing shows the landing's rail. The shape of its posts is our guess.

The photo shows a door with panels, up straight steps between stone side walls. We read the door off the photo. It has one dark door, about a meter across. Over it is a window of two panes with a gently curved top.
The drawing shows a steep slate roof behind the bay's pointed top. Our plain four-slope roof is a fair stand-in. The pointed top over the bay is left for later work.

In the photo, the main roof rises behind the front gable. Its top line runs back from the street. It is slate, with a window sticking out on its south slope. Our roof stands behind the gable, and its front slope runs into it.

A raised main floor sits over a basement. It is inside our usual range. The old map draws a stone porch at the door, which is the landing at the top of the steps. The plan for this house asks for high steps. It fits a whole number of steps. No paper or picture gives its height.

The landing is short, because the front yard is only 3.85 meters deep. The steps now come down sideways, along the front. So the landing runs along the front too. This number is kept to check that the steps fit, and they do.

A steep slate roof sits over the edge, its sides a little curved. Windows stick out of it where the photo shows them. Two are on the front and one is on the south side. They have square tops under small peaks. We did not carve their sides. Iron trim runs along the edge of the flat top.

A small square tower with slatted sides sits on the stable's roof. A pointed roof and a knob top it. Photos from 1888 and 1963 show it. Every size is our guess, read from the photo. It is about 6 feet square. We think it was still there in 1904, because no paper says it was taken off.
The photo and an old drawing from 1886 show an iron fence with spear tips. It stands on a stone curb along the walk. The gates are our guess. The fence along 20th Street is left for later work.
This house has a stone front. Its side and back walls are plain brick. No picture shows which kind of brick. We gave it a pinkish brick, so the plain brick on the street is not all the same.

This house has a stone front. Its side and back walls are plain brick. No picture shows which kind of brick. We gave it a brick darkened by smoke, so the plain brick on the street is not all the same.
This house has a stone front. Its side and back walls are plain brick. No picture shows which kind of brick. We gave it a yellow brick, so the plain brick on the street is not all the same.

A stone gable faces 18th Street. Over the loft door is an arch of wedge-shaped stones. Photos from 1888 and 1963 show it. The owner of this project looked at it next to an old print. The tiles run over the gable's edges and end in a thin line. No stone cap stands above the roof. The photo from 1963 shows the same thin edge.

A stone gable wall faces 18th Street. Its top rises from the corners to a chimney in the middle. Photos from 1888 and 1963 show it. We read its height above the roof off the 1888 photo, good to about half a foot. The stone top stops at the chimney's sides. The chimney's own face rises there, with the date stones on it.

A tall, steep slate roof sits over the edge. The old picture from 1893 puts its bend about 5 meters up. We built it at 4.5 meters, the highest our plan allows. Windows stick out of it where the picture shows them. Three are on the front and a big one is on the corner.

This says where the house stands, read off the old fire map. The front wall is about 8 meters long. A bay with angled sides sticks out of it. The house runs back about 23 meters on its south part and 13 on its north part. The map draws one front line, so where the two parts meet is our guess.

This says where the building stands, read off the old fire map. The map draws its walls from the alley. It is about 11 meters deep and about 10 meters along the alley. So it is nearly square, a little deeper than long.

This says where the building stands, read off the old fire map. Its shape leans a little, like a pushed box. It is about 15 meters long. Its west and east walls run almost side by side. The east wall follows the railroad's edge.

This says where the building stands, read off the old fire map. Its shape leans a little, like a pushed box. It is about 17 meters long, from one lot line to the other. Its west and east walls run almost side by side. The east wall follows the railroad's edge.

This says where things sit along the front, from the north wall. The door is under the porch. A column of windows stands south of the tall front part. We moved that column a little, after reading the picture again. Its roof window moved with it.

As the photo shows, an iron fence on a stone curb stands along the walk. Its panels have curly shapes. There is no side gate. The north side stands too close to the lot line for a path. Workers reached the back from 20th Street.

A photo from about 1897 shows an iron fence on a stone curb in front of the house. It has round posts. The gates and the side gate are our guesses. The front gates stand open into the yard. No picture shows them open or shut.
The basement has small windows in the front wall. They sit under the raised main floor. The old map does not mark a basement. So the basement is our guess.
The stone is left bare. Nothing says the house was painted or washed white. The photo from 1888 shows the cut stone itself.
Small basement windows sit low on the side wall. We read them off an old drawing. The ones on the front, under the tall front part, have iron bars.

This says where the bays sit along the front, from north to south. First is the curved bay. Then comes the door, in the middle of the wall between that bay and the side wing. The owner of this project set it there. The old drawing shows the door and the window over it in the middle of that wall.

The front is a pale stone from Bedford, in Indiana. Our list gives that stone for 1801. It is laid in smooth rows, as the photo shows on the front and the side. Two rows of stone make the base. The carved bands and trim are left for later work.

This is the glass house that Beman built in 1892, as a photo by J. W. Taylor shows it. It is a round room of glass between seven stone columns, on a stone base. A railing runs round its flat top. A ribbed dome rises over it, with a knob on top. Each height is within about a third of a meter of the photo. The glass, frame and plants come from our plan for glass houses.

This is Beman's glass house, as a picture from 1894 and a photo from about 1897 show it. It is a long glass hall with a pointed top. It stands on a stone base. A stone doorway with an arch sits in its north end. A pointed glass wing crosses it in the middle.

Both photos show a deep roof edge painted a light color across the pair. A row of small blocks runs under it. We built it with small brackets to stand for those blocks. They stand further apart than in the photo. The paint is white. It looks as bright as the porch columns in each picture, the way white paint does.

Both photos show chimneys on the roof. The owner of this project looked closely. There is one wide chimney on the shared wall between the two houses, just behind the railing. There is one more on each outer end wall. Where they stand and how tall they are is partly our guess.

Both photos show each house's door under a stone porch at its outer end. Four columns stand along its front. On top is an iron railing round a little balcony. We worked out the porch's depth from the two photos. Where the steps go is our guess. The porch is painted wood, white like the roof edge, not stone.

Both photos show one rain pipe down the front, on the line between the two houses. The gutter and the back pipe are our guesses. The owner of this project looked closely. Both houses' gutters drain to that one pipe.

Both photos show the tops of the upper windows laid in brick, with a stone block in the middle. There is no stone beam over them. The owner of this project pointed this out. So the tops are now flat rows of brick, each with its stone block. We sized the blocks from the photo.

The front is brownstone, as our list gives for 1729. It is laid in smooth rows, as the photo shows on both street sides. The trim is cut from the same brownstone, all one color. The owner of this project said the walls looked like red brick. So we laid them in the brown stone.

George H. Wheeler built this house. A paper from June 7, 1884 gives his building permit for a three floor house. A photo from about 1885 to 1900 shows it. The old fire map of 1911 draws it too. So it stood in 1904.

This says where the windows sit along the front, from the north end. One column stands behind the bay. The entrance arch's middle we read off an old picture from 1888. The small strip north of the bay is gone. The picture shows it is the bay's angled side.

A photo from after 1902 shows 1700's front open to its lawn south of its steps. A low stone edge runs there. North of the steps, an iron railing with spear tips runs on a low curb. It matches the one at 1706, since the pair are mirror images. We built the railing just inside the street line.

A photo from after 1902 shows an iron railing with spear tips on a low curb. It runs along 1706's front to two stone posts at the walk, and stops there. North of the walk, the front lies open to its lawn behind a low stone edge, like 1700's. We built the railing just inside the street line, clear of the sidewalk.

We read the roof off an old photo. Its steep lower sides rise straight from the roof edge to a bend about 12 meters up. Each house has two roof windows with small peaks over them. The two houses' windows are not set the same way.

In the old photo, the front's brick is darker than its slate roof. That means a red brick. It is much darker than the white trim. The side wall looks paler. So the front is a pressed red brick, and the sides are a plain pale brick.

A photo shows a small iron balcony on a stone shelf before each round-topped window. It is a little wider than the window. We did not build its diamond pattern. Plain bars stand in. The window runs down behind it to just above the shelf, as the photos show.

Copper gutters run along the roof, with two rain pipes by the front corners. The drawing shows no pipe down the front. So the pipes hang on the sides, a little back from the front corners. That matches a photo of 1625. Where they stand is our guess, since the drawing shows neither side.

Three lines of letters are cut in the stone block, under the front panel. They look pale on the granite in an old photo. We sized each line from the photo. The letters are plain capitals, squeezed to fit. They are not the cutter's own style.

We dressed this house to match its three pictures. A small railing tops the little lookout tower. Iron trim runs round the flat roof, with a thin spike at each corner. A stone band runs under the upper floor.

The windows slide up and down. Every size fits our usual window ranges. The main floor's windows are tall, as in the old picture. The third floor's match the picture's arched windows. The side and back walls take the same rows. Nothing shows those walls.

Both maps color this building pink, which means brick. They also give the walls' thickness. An old drawing from 1874 shows a wooden building here. We think that was the wooden stable the brick one replaced.

We read every window of the front off the old picture from 1888. Two tall windows sit on the ground floor beside the porch. Above them, the second and third floors each have three windows, a wide one between two narrow ones. The third floor's wide window rises under a round arch.

We read every front window off the photo. The ground floor has a wide window of two parts. A small window sits beside the bay. The third floor has a pair of windows. Each sits in a stone frame of long and short blocks, as the photo shows.

Every window on the street side has a round top. A picture from 1893 shows them. The basement has a pair of small round-topped windows under each outer bay. The main floor has a pair of round-topped windows under one arch in each outer bay.

In the photo, every street window sits under a carved stone hood. Now the front windows have round tops. Each has an arch band and a stone in the middle. The square windows elsewhere keep a flat stone hood.
In the photo, every street window has a gently curved top under a light stone hood. A small stone block sits in the middle of each. The photo's hoods end in short ears, which we did not carve.
As the photo shows, every street window has a stone hood on both floors. The window on the south side wears the same hood. Each hood has carved curls on top, about a meter wide.
A paper from 1869 says every window had brown stone trim. The photo shows heavy carved hoods over the main windows. The upper windows have tall carved hoods with curls on top.

Every window in the front has a round top. We read them off the photo. The upper floor has a pair of windows in each bay. The main floor has one tall window in each outer bay. The basement has a pair of small windows under each outer bay.

Every window comes from our window plan. They slide up and down, with two panes over two. The basement windows sit just above the ground. No picture shows the panes of these windows. Two over two was the most common kind, so it is our guess.
In the old picture, every front window sits in a light stone frame with a carved head. The upper windows have carved curls on top. The band under the roof has pairs of carved rings.

The family moved in in December 1887. A photo from early 1888 shows the house done outside. The first change outside came in 1946. That year it became a place for research. The scene shows the house as it stood on 1 July 1904.

At the south end of the front is a bay with angled sides. It rises through both floors and up into a tall slate roof of its own. Photos from the middle of the last century and from 2024 show the same. We read its shape off the photo.

We read the monument's base off a photo from 1893 by J. W. Taylor. It is the one picture that shows a side of the stone base. We matched fourteen corners on the front and the side. That gave how deep each step of the base is.

We read the monument's base off a photo from 1893 by J. W. Taylor. It is the one picture that shows a side of the stone base. We matched fourteen corners on the front and the side. That gave how deep each step of the base is.

We read the monument's base off a photo from 1893 by J. W. Taylor. It is the one picture that shows a side of the stone base. We matched fourteen corners on the front and the side. That gave how deep each step of the base is.
Flat stone beams sit over every front window. The photo shows them on the ground and first floors. The second floor's tops are gently curved. The big window over the door has a carved hood.

We read the floor heights off the photo. A stone band over the first floor stands about 5.6 meters up. The balcony's floor is about 9.5 meters up. The third floor's two arched windows rise to about 12 meters. The wall's top is set just above them. The gable stands on it.
We read the floor heights off the photo. The second floor's windows sit about 7 meters up. The top of the wall is about 10 meters up. Over it, a plain band and the roof edge rise to about 11 meters.

Each floor is a little shorter than the one below. The heights fit our usual ranges. The top of the wall is 15.4 meters up, a bit more than 1615's. So the two fronts do not line up across the path between them. No paper or picture gives this house's heights.
Each floor is a little shorter than the one below. There are four floors, at our usual starting heights. The top of the wall is 15.2 meters up. No paper or picture gives this house's heights.

Each floor is a little shorter than the one below. There are four floors, the same as 1613's. So the pair's floors, windows and roof edge line up across their shared wall. No paper or picture gives this house's heights.
Each floor is a little shorter than the one below, at our usual starting heights. No paper or picture gives this house's heights.

We read the floor heights off the photo. The first floor's windows sit about 4 meters up. The second floor's sit about 8 meters up. The gable's windows are higher still. So the floors stand at about 3.6, 7.2 and 11 meters.
Each floor's height is the same as 1628's, inside our usual ranges. The top of the wall stands 12.3 meters up.

We read the floor heights off the photo. The upper floor's windows sit about 7.6 meters up. The stone stops at about 10.6 meters. A band with small windows runs above it, up to the roof edge. One book calls the house three floors, counting that band as an attic.
The main floor is the tallest. The upper floor is a bit taller than our first try. That way its windows and the bracketed roof edge both fit. No paper or picture gives this house's heights.

We read the floor heights off the photo's windows and stone bands. The second floor is about 5.3 meters up. The third floor is about 9.2 meters up. We made the third floor a little shorter, so the side walls end at the right height.

We read the floor heights off the photo's windows. The second floor is about 6.2 meters up. The side walls stop at about 10.6 meters. These are tall floors for a row house. The pictures show them taller than the house next door.

The house has four stone chimneys. The old drawings give the height of each top. A photo from 1888 shows all four. We moved the north chimney's face a little, so it lines up with the gable's face, as the drawing shows.
Four windows on each floor run along the south wall, by the path. Now the wall is longer. So there is one window every 4 meters along it. Their places are our guess.

A book from 1923 names a dark finish for the iron. The front door's grille and the carriage door's straps, rings and hinges use our dark iron. Its exact color and roughness are our guesses. Black and white photos can not show a finish.

A book from 1923 says vines were planted in 1887. A photo from 1888 shows bare walls. A photo from about 1923 shows vine stems in the courtyard. How much vine grew by 1904 is not known. So our summer vines are our own guess.

Old survey photos show a flat north gable that runs into a half-round tower on the west. It is not a whole round tower, as we once thought. Its pointed roof is about 10 feet tall, with a little flared skirt. These sizes come from the photos, not a new survey.

A survey from 1963 says the roof over the curved front hall is covered in copper. We think it was copper in 1904 too. Nothing says it changed. The drawings show a short, low roof over the curve. An older guess of its shape has been replaced, read again from the drawing.

The old survey drawing prints the house's full size, so we can check our scan. It gives the curved wall's inside size. The outside wall is about 10.6 feet out. We fixed an older reading that put it in the wrong place. The door and windows stay where they were.

The old survey drawing shows round sunk shapes and square panels on each carriage door. It shows the paired ring plates too. A paper describes the same heavy doors, with straps and latches. Older photos were used only to check. The doors now carry the panels, three straps each, rings and hinges. Their exact depths are our guesses.

Round gutters and rain pipes run at the front's two corners. The photo shows a pipe down the front's north edge, by the house next door. Another stands at the south corner. That one sits just behind the front corner, where the photo shows it.

We placed these windows off the plans. Their heights come from counting the rows of stone on the old survey drawing. One row was copied wrong before. Fixing it lowers the top of the window by one inch.

The heights come from the old drawing. We once guessed where the top of the north gable sits. Now the old photos place it better. Where the roofs meet behind it is our guess. There is no survey drawing of that side.

A photo from about 1887 and old drawings show a stone edge round the lawn by the house. They show gaps for the way in. We think it was still there in 1904. The edging stops at the main door and the carriage porch. Its size and the space between its joints are our guesses.

The drawing does not show how far the roof windows stand out from the slope. So we set them a little back from the roof's edge. Their sides run back into the slope. We moved them to fit the old photos better.

We worked this out from a drawing of 1893. The stone band under the main floor sits about a quarter of the way up the front. That means a high basement. It works out to about 2.4 meters. We built it at 2.3 meters. The drawing gives the shape, not the true size.
We worked this out from a drawing of 1893. It shows a low roof of four slopes. The roof's top stands only a little above the roof edge. So the slope must be gentle, about 18 degrees.
We worked these out from a drawing of 1893. The main floor's stone band is about 2.4 meters up. The upper windows are about 6 meters up. The top of the wall is about 10.7 meters up.

The sides and back are brick, as the old fire map colors them. Old photos show the walls painted a light color. One book says the paint was over a plaster coat. So we used a pale paint that covers the brick.
Copper gutters run along the roof, with two rain pipes. The photo does not see these walls. We moved the pipes a little, clear of the corner brackets. Where they stand is our guess.
Copper gutters run along the roof, with two rain pipes. No picture shows them. Each pipe stands a little way back from a front corner, clear of the brackets above.
Copper gutters run along the roof, with two rain pipes. No picture shows them. The south pipe stands behind the stone part at the front of that side. An old photo shows no pipe on that stone part.

The roof is flat. It slopes a little to the back, behind low walls with stone tops. Our rules give the pair the same roof. So both houses stand under one roof line. No paper or picture shows this roof.
The roof is flat. It slopes a little to the back, behind low walls with stone tops. Our rules give stone-front houses like this a flat roof. No paper or picture shows this roof.

The roof is flat. It slopes a little to the back, behind low walls with stone tops. That is our rule for a brick row house four floors high. A sloped roof on this narrow house would stick up almost 2 meters. No paper or picture shows that either.
The roof is flat. It slopes a little to the back, behind low walls with stone tops. A long, narrow brick house three floors high often had a flat roof. No paper or picture shows the roof.
The roof is flat. It slopes a little to the back, behind low walls with stone tops. A narrow row house three floors high, sharing a wall, often had a flat roof. No paper or picture shows the roof.
The roof is flat. It slopes a little to the back, behind low walls with stone tops. A narrow row house three floors high, sharing a wall, often had a flat roof. No paper or picture shows the roof.

A round copper gutter runs along the roof's edge. Copper pipes drain it to flat stones on the ground. One is at the front's north corner. One is on the south wall. Two are on the back wall. The back part's flat top has no gutter. All of this is our guess.

A round copper gutter runs along the roof's edge. Copper pipes drain it to flat stones on the ground. One is at the front's south corner. One is in the middle of the south wall. Two are on the back wall. The back part's flat top has no gutter. All of this is our guess.

The side and back walls have windows of two panes over two. Under the main floor's arch is a wide window. Its top is glass in a pattern of small squares, as the drawing shows. Below it is a wide, low arched window for the basement.

The doorway is deep, with a round-topped hole. A pair of doors with panels sits back in it, under a fan-shaped window. Stone blocks ring the arch. The old drawing shows a round-arched doorway set back in the wall.
A door with panels sits at the top of a few steps. The front yard is less than 4 meters deep. The photo shows a flat-topped doorway in a stone frame, under a carved panel.
A door with panels sits at the top of straight steps. The front yard is as deep as 1634's, since the two fronts line up.
A door with panels sits at the top of straight steps. The front yard runs from the house to the street line.

A door with panels sits up a flight of steps. The front stands about 10 meters back from the street. The steps climb from the north, along the front, to a landing by the door. Both pictures show it that way. Under the landing is a round-arched basement door with bars.

A round-topped doorway sits at the top of straight steps in the middle bay. It is about 1.3 meters across. A ring of stones runs over it, like the windows beside it. The steps are open, with a rail on each side. A drawing from 1893 shows it that way.

We gave the front windows no stone hoods. Each one is copied from an old print. They have round arches. The side walls keep plain stone beams. The photo's arched windows on the 18th Street side are left for later work.
We gave the front windows no stone hoods. Each one is copied from the photo. The arched ones have rings of stone. The stone bands and carved knobs are left for later work.

The windows of the front's north part have small stone roofs over them, on both floors. Both pictures show carved tops there. Their exact shape is our guess. The same kind of top sits over the door, as the old drawing shows.

Two old books say the courtyard walls were plain brick of a slightly pink color. The exact color is ours. It is a warm red brown, pushed toward pink. It is not the brick of the 1835 town, which came from a different building.

A survey from 1963 records copper on the roof over the curved hall. By 1904 it had been out in coal smoke for seventeen years. So we made it a dark brown, not shiny new copper or full green. The same color is used for the knobs on top and the dining bay's roof.
The roof is low, as the old photo shows. Its slope is 34 degrees. At that slope our roof plan joins a long house's roof cleanly. The photo does not show it more exactly.

The roof is low, with four slopes. It is just high enough to hold the attic the old map marks with a half. A window in the roof lights it from the street. At this slope our plan joins the roof cleanly. It is tin, not slate, because our slate is cut for a steeper roof.

The roof is low, with four slopes, over a full third floor. There is no attic to light. At this slope our plan joins the roof cleanly. It is tin, not slate, because our slate is cut for a steeper roof.

The roof is low, with four slopes, over a full third floor. There is no attic to light. At this slope our plan joins the roof cleanly. It is tin, not slate, because our slate is cut for a steeper roof.

Nine steps lead up to the door, as the old picture from 1888 shows. Each is 15 centimeters high, so the floor is 1.35 meters up. The bay's ground floor windows are 2 meters up. The floor stays low enough that the door clears the bay window above.

No survey drawing shows the 18th Street side. So we placed its windows by the gaps in the stone on the floor plans. The great arch and the big window over it have their own heights, from the drawings. A photo from 1963 shows the same row of narrow windows.

We built no fence or wall across the front. No picture of this front exists, and our first try had none. One big lot held 2000, 2010 and 2018. So where this house's yard ends to the north is our guess.
We built no fence or wall across the front. No picture of this front or its pair exists, and our first try had none. The lot's sides come from the street map.
We built no fence or wall across the front. No picture of this front or its pair exists, and our first try had none. The lot's sides come from the street map.
There is no bracketed or carved roof edge across the front. The photo shows a plain stone band at about 10.5 meters up. The slate roof's edge sits over it. The small tower's top rises past it.

There is no roof edge across the front. The photo shows the front rising into the shaped gable with no edge across it. No picture shows the tops of the side walls. So they run plain, with only a tiny overhang, like 1625's. Before, a bracketed wooden edge stood here.

We built no gutter or rain pipe. The drawing shows none on the front. The roof's side walls rise past it, so our gutter has nowhere to hang. How the roof drained is not known. The earlier copper gutters were our guesses too, so they are gone with that roof.
The photo shows no gutter or pipe on the front. We hang none on this kind of roof yet.
No picture shows this house's brick. It was built about 1890, when golden yellow pressed brick fronts were in fashion. So the front is that brick. The sides are a plain yellow brick.

No picture shows this house's brick. It was built in the 1860s. Then, cream brick from Milwaukee was the city's front brick. Red pressed fronts had not come in yet. So the front is cream brick, greyed by 1904's smoke. The sides are a plain pinkish brick.

No picture shows this house's brick. It was built in the 1860s. Then, cream brick from Milwaukee was the city's front brick. Red pressed fronts had not come in yet. So the front is cream brick, greyed by 1904's smoke. The sides are a plain brick darkened by smoke.

No picture shows this house's brick. The front is a pressed brown brick, like other brick fronts of its time on the street. The photos of the street show dark fronts over paler sides. The sides are a plain pale brick.

No picture shows this house's brick. The front is a pressed red brick, like other brick fronts of its time on the street. The photos of the street show red fronts over paler sides. The sides are a plain pinkish brick.

No picture shows this house's brick. The front is a pressed red brick, like other brick fronts of its time on the street. The owner of this project looked at the pale north side round its red bay. The owner said the bay should be red brick all around, the same as the front. So now it is.

No picture shows this house's brick. The front is a pressed red brick, like other brick fronts of its time on the street. The photos of the street show red fronts over paler sides. The sides are a plain yellow brick.

No picture shows this house's brick. The front is a deep red pressed brick, like other brick fronts of its time on the street. The photos of the street show red fronts over paler sides. The sides are a plain pinkish brick.

No picture shows this house's brick. The front is a deep red pressed brick, like other brick fronts of its time on the street. The photos of the street show red fronts over paler sides. The sides are a plain yellow brick.
No picture shows the side walls. Their windows are left for later work.

No drawing shows the gate or its post from the front. So the short wall, the pair of closed oak doors and the tall post are our guesses. They are kept lower than the tunnel at the other end of the same carriage way.

No drawing shows this wall from the side. A photo from about 1923 shows only the wall next door. So its height of 9 feet is our guess. It matches the wall by the alley gate, so the two meet at one line. Its stone top is the same as the gate's.

There is no window on the south side between its bay and the front corner. We took out the two that were there. An old photo shows that edge as plain stone with no window. No picture shows the side behind the bay.
We put no windows in either side wall. One side stands against 2001, as the old map shows. The other side is a wall shared with 2005. So both are built blank.
We put no windows in either side wall. One side is a wall shared with 2003. The other stands very close to 2007, as the old map shows. So both are built blank.
There is none. The old map shows a part four floors high beside the back of the main house. It sticks out to the south. A plain back wing can not do that. So it is now built as its own back part.

The old map and street plan put this lot on the corner of 18th Street and Prairie Avenue. The house's north side stands on the 18th Street line. Its east side stands about 4.5 meters back from Prairie Avenue. That is read off the same map, give or take about half a meter.

We built one box round the L-shaped plan in the old picture. The picture shows a main part and a shallower part along the front. One box fills the gap the picture leaves at the back corner. Our plan can not leave that gap yet.

We built one box round the outline on the old map. It holds the front house, its stone front and north wing, and the back wing of two floors. One box fills in the small courtyard the map shows at one corner. Our plan can not leave that gap yet.

There is one window on the south side, between its bay and the front corner. It sits next to the bay, as the photo shows. The photo shows it on the upper floor only, with plain brick below it. Before, we had a window on each floor there.
This version gets the more detailed model. Its roughness, glass, woodwork and sizes are our guesses, kept inside what the drawings and photos show. Its shape is not a new fact about the house.
An old picture from 1890 shows a hanging lamp just south of the porch. It is a dark bell shape, about 0.7 meters across and 1 meter tall. It hangs between two banded posts. We added it there.

The owner of this project looked at an old print beside the model. The alley gable is stone under a thin roof edge, not a wall rising above the roof. The print shows the tiles running over its edges. So the roof now runs a little past the wall, and the wall follows the tiles up.

This was the one finished house on the block with no walk to its door. The photo shows a light walk running straight from the sidewalk, between two square posts in the low wall, to the foot of the steps. Lawn lies behind the wall on each side. So we laid a walk of flat stones there, 2.5 meters wide.

The owner of this project asked that every house have a walk to its door. The drawing shows the steps coming down to the ground in front of the house, with no fence. So the walk runs in stone squares from the foot of the steps, 1.7 meters wide, straight out to the sidewalk. Grass covers the rest of the front yard. The drawing does not show the walk's line or what it was made of. The walk's stone squares, its width and wear, and the grass are our guesses.

The owner of this project asked that every house have a walk to its door. A picture of Spalding's house shows the steps coming down between the end of the garden wall and the first post of the iron fence. A light walk curves out to the street. So the walk runs in stone squares, 1.8 meters wide, from the steps out through that gap to the sidewalk. We made it straight where the picture curves it. Grass covers the garden. No side gate is drawn, so there is no side walk. The walk's stone squares, its width and wear, and the grass are our guesses.

The owner of this project asked that every house have a walk to its door. The photo shows the ground in front of the door paved up to the step, lighter than the yard on each side, with nothing across the front. So the walk runs in stone squares, 1.6 meters wide, straight out to the sidewalk. Grass covers the rest. The photo is too worn and far off to show the squares or the width. The walk's stone squares, its width and wear, and the grass are our guesses.

The owner of this project asked that every house have a walk to its door. No picture of this front is kept. Every pictured front on this side of the 1600 block is closed at the street and open only at the walk. 1612 has an iron fence with spear tops, 1620 an iron lattice, 1616 boards, and 1638, the block's other wood house, iron bars on a low stone base. So we closed this front the same way. A low stone edge runs along the street line, with an iron rail on it, as at 1638. There is a gap, 1.5 meters wide, in line with the porch steps, between two stone posts, with no gate in it. The kind of edge, its height, the posts and the gap are our guesses.

The owner of this project asked that every house have a walk to its door. No picture of 1616's own front is kept. A picture of 1620 from May 1874 shows only part of its board fence. So we laid the walk like the block's pictured fronts. A photo of 1612 shows a light paved walk from the sidewalk, through an open gate, to the steps. So this walk runs in stone squares from the steps, through the gate in the boards, to the sidewalk. Grass covers the rest of the front yard. The picture shows the boards with no break at the side, so there is no side gate or side walk. The walk's stone squares, its width and wear, and the grass are our guesses.

The owner of this project asked that every house have a walk to its door. Both pictures, one from 1874 and one from 1898, show the steps coming straight down to the street between the gate posts. So the front walk is a short run in stone squares from the steps, through the gate, to the sidewalk. A side walk of cinders runs from the side gate, across the side yard, back to the house's back corner. Grass covers the rest of the front yard, with bare dirt under the open stair. Neither picture shows the ground. So the squares, the cinders and the grass are our guesses, aged to 1904.

The owner of this project asked that every house have a walk to its door. The drawing shows the side steps coming down in front of the house, with no fence. So the walk runs in stone squares from the steps, 1.2 meters wide, straight out to the sidewalk. Grass covers the rest of the front yard. The drawing does not show the walk's line or what it was made of. The walk's stone squares, its width and wear, and the grass are our guesses.

The owner of this project asked that every house have a walk to its door. A photo of 1612 shows a light paved walk from the sidewalk to the foot of the steps. The fence's gate stands open there, with two people at the foot of the stair. Inside the fence the yard is low, with a bush at the south end. So the front walk runs in stone squares from the steps, through the gate, to the sidewalk. A side walk of cinders runs back down the narrow south side to the house's back corner. Grass covers the rest of the front yard. The photo shows the walk is paved, but not what it is made of, and does not see the side. So the squares, the cinders and the grass are our guesses. We are not sure we may use the photo, so the yard's size comes from the 1911 map.

The owner of this project asked that every house have a walk to its door. No picture of 1600's front is kept. So we laid its walk like the other houses on this block that do have pictures. A photo of 1612 shows a light paved walk from the sidewalk, through an open gate, to the steps. So this walk runs in stone squares from the foot of the steps, through the gate, to the sidewalk. Grass covers the rest of the front yard, inside the iron fence. We did not add a side walk, since no picture shows one. The walk's stone squares, its width and wear, and the grass are our guesses.

The owner of this project asked that every house have a walk to its door. The walk at 1638 starts at the foot of the porch stair. It runs along the back of the fence, past the gate posts, and out through the gate to the street. It is made of stone squares like the posts' stone. A photo shows pale ground in the gateway and at the foot of the stair, behind the fence. The bushes hide the rest of the yard. So the walk's line along the fence, its width of 1.2 meters, and the squares are our guesses.

The owner of this project asked that every house have a walk to its door. A photo shows 1700's steps coming down by the start of the railing. So the walk runs in stone squares from the steps, through the gate, to the sidewalk. The pair of houses has no side passage, so there is no side walk. The walk's stone squares, its width and wear, and the grass are our guesses.

The owner of this project asked that every house have a walk to its door. A photo shows 1706's walk coming out from its steps, between the posts, to the sidewalk. So the walk runs in stone squares from the steps, through the gate. The pair of houses has no side passage, so there is no side walk. The walk's stone squares, its width and wear, and the grass are our guesses.

The owner of this project asked that every house have a walk to its door. No picture shows 1712's front yard close enough to say what was round it. The small map of 1893 is too tiny to read, and photos from 1939 to 1942 show the Kodak plant that took its place. So we built the block's own kind: a low stone edge on the street line, about a third of a meter high, like the ones at 1700, 1721 and 1736. It has a gap for the walk, straight out from the steps, which sit in the middle, as the 1893 drawing shows. The kind, the height and the gap are our guesses.

The owner of this project asked that every house have a walk to its door. No picture of 1812 shows an iron fence. Levy's photo shows the stair running down to the walk with nothing across its foot. A view from about 1888 shows low pale stone blocks in front of the stair, like at 1808 next door. So we built a low stone wall, about a third of a meter high, on the street line, with a gap at the stair. The house fills its lot, so there is no side passage. The wall's height and shape are our guesses from that small view.

The owner of this project asked that every house have a walk to its door. No picture shows 1709's front yard close enough to say what was round it. The small map of 1893 draws the house behind its trees and lamp posts, too small to read. So we built the block's own kind: a low stone edge on the street line, about a third of a meter high, like the ones at 1700, 1721 and 1736. It has a gap for the walk, straight out from the steps. The kind, the height and the gap are our guesses.

The owner of this project asked that every house have a walk to its door. A photo from about 1895 shows no fence. A low stone edge, about a foot high, runs round the raised lawn. It runs along Prairie Avenue and 18th Street. The walk from the steps passes through it to the sidewalk. We built that low stone wall, with a gap for the walk. South of the house, no picture of 1904 shows it, so that part is our guess.

The owner of this project asked that every house have a walk to its door. A picture from 1883 shows a low line along the walk before the house. It breaks where the walk comes out from the side steps, with a post at the break. It shows no iron fence. So we built a low stone wall, with a gap and a post on each side. The posts and the wall's shape are our guesses, because the picture is small.

The owner of this project asked that every house have a walk to its door. A newspaper picture from 1898 shows the steps coming down under an arched porch. It shows no fence or gate, but it is cut off at the foot of the steps. So we built the low stone wall the other houses on the block have, with a gap for the walk. Its kind, height and gap are our guesses.

The owner of this project asked that every house have a walk to its door. A winter photo from about 1888 shows a low stone wall along the street. It has a gap for the walk, with a stone post on each side. So we built that, along the sidewalk's edge. Its shape, the gap's width and the posts' size are our guesses.

The owner of this project asked that every house have a walk to its door. The only picture of 1730 from its own time is from May 1874. It shows a fence of boards along the whole street, with no gate. So we built a board fence, 1.5 meters high. The gate on the walk and the side gate are our own. The fence lasting to 1904, its height and both gates are our guesses.

The owner of this project asked that every house have a walk to its door. The photo shows the walk leaving the steps and curving north behind the low wall, to its gap at the north end. A round flower bed sits in the bend. We built a walk of flat stones there, 1.2 meters wide. We made the curve as two square turns. The stones and the lawn are our guesses.

The owner of this project asked that every house have a walk to its door. The photo shows no fence. A low wall of rough brownstone runs along the lot line. It has a gap for the walk and another at the south path, with a stone block between them. Three old pictures agree on this order. So the walk leaves the steps and turns south behind the wall to its gap. No walk runs through to the south path.

The owner of this project asked that every house have a walk to its door. The side steps end running north along the front. The walk leaves them there and goes out through the wall's gap to the sidewalk. It is 1.5 meters wide, with lawn on each side. The walk's stones and the lawn are our guesses.

The owner of this project asked that every house have a walk to its door. The front photo shows no fence. A low stone wall runs along the sidewalk. A square stone post stands on each side of the walk. So we built them, close to where the photo puts them. The photo also shows a low iron railing across the north side yard. We built that too, on a small curb.

Every picture of the house shows it on a pale stone basement. The stone runs from the ground up to the main floor, about 2 meters up. Its round-topped windows are cut in it. The brick starts above it. All the pictures show the basement as light as the window frames. So we built the base in smooth pale stone.

Two old pictures show the same pale stone basement going round the angled corner. It runs along the south side too, with brick above it. No picture shows the north side. So that side stays brick down to the ground.

A newspaper photo from about 1905 is the closest picture to 1904. It shows a tall iron fence with spear tips on a stone curb. It runs along the street and round the south yard. It is almost 2 meters high, on iron posts. So we built that fence, with its gates as tall.

The old drawings show a wide stone top and a thinner row below on the street chimneys. An early photo agrees. The exact sizes are our guesses, read from scans. Photos from 2024 show two brick chimneys with plain pale stone tops. Giving them that look in 1904 is our guess.

An early photo shows boxes at the tops of the rain pipes on the Prairie side, and wide straps. Survey photos show where the small pipes run. Later pipes tell us the routes, not the exact pipes of 1904. Their sizes, their carving and the hidden joints are our guesses.
We read this off an old picture from 1894 again. The lodge's north front has a tall ground floor. It is an open porch of three openings between round columns. A band for a balcony runs above it.
A photo from about 1895 shows a porch in the corner, at the front's 18th Street end. It has a round arch on the front and one on the side. Each is about 2 meters across. We built it from the photo.

We worked out the paths from the gate, passage and stair on the old survey drawing. The drive now runs straight between the gate and the passage. The plan does not show how the ground was paved in 1904. The narrow foot paths, their pale gravel and the lawn's edge are our guesses.

An old picture from 1894 shows the lodge's north front in rough stone, like the part next to it. It is not brick. The 1911 map colors one corner pink, but we think that was a slip. The map's two floors stand.

We read the old survey photos again. One window we added was a copy of one already there. So we took it out. The photos also show one narrow attic window just east of the tower. Its size is our guess, read from the photos.

This whole part is our guess. Its big chimney on the 18th Street side we read off a photo by J. W. Taylor. It is a stone chimney that stands on the roof edge and runs up the steep roof.

We read this off the front photo and the 1911 map. A tall part stands across the north end of the front. It rises an extra floor past the main roof edge, under its own steep roof. On the north side there is a part for the stairs, and on the south side a slanted bay. The 1911 map has no corner bay. The house was changed in 1902, so which is right for 1904 is still an open question. Later work set the corner bay out about two and a half feet past the main front's south wall. Both old pictures show it that way. So the main wall moves in, and the bay stays where it was.

We read the windows off an old photo. The main floor's windows are about 1.2 meters wide, with arched tops. The upper floor's are a little narrower. A photo from 1901, before the glass was in, shows the main windows start about 1.4 meters up.
We read this off two old photos. The second floor's windows are about 5.7 meters up. The third floor's are about 9.2 meters up. The third floor runs up to the roof edge, about 13 meters up.
We read this off the pair's front. The upper windows sit about 5.5 meters up. The main floor's arches top out at about 4.9 meters. The roof edge is about 8.3 meters up.

We read this off a photo and the old map. The front's south part has three floors of wall, up to 13.2 meters. It lines up with the south corner, as the photo shows. We moved its north side a little, to meet the curved bay.

We read this off the 1888 picture. The second floor stands near 5 meters up. The roof floor stands near 8.4 meters up. The roof's front slope comes down behind the bay. So the third floor is up in the roof.

We read this off the old drawing. The main floor has one broad window with a round arch. Its sill is about 2.1 meters up. Long stones ring the arch. Under it is a broad, low basement window behind an iron grille.

We read this off the old drawing. The arched window's middle is about 1.55 meters from the north wall. The door's arch is about 4.6 meters from it. The bay window above stands clear of both arches. A third, blank bay is there so our plan can build the front.
We read this off the photo. The porch's balcony floor is about 6.6 meters up. The steps rise about 2 meters from the walk.
We read this off the photo. The landing at the door is about 1.67 meters above the walk. The steps rise to it in about seven steps.
We read this off the photo. The main floor's windows are about 2.55 meters tall. The upper floor's are about 2.15 meters. These are taller than we usually start.

We read this off the photo. The main floor's windows run from about 2.5 to 5.4 meters up. The upper floor's run from about 6.7 to 9.2 meters up. The brackets start about 10.4 meters up, under a roof edge about 11.7 meters up.

We read the roof off the photo. Its steep sides rise from the roof edge, 8.1 meters up, to a bend about 7 meters higher. That is a very tall roof. It holds the third floor and an attic. The roof windows and the iron trim on top are left for later work.

We read this off the photo. A band over the main floor sits about 5 meters up. We made the second floor taller, so the roof edge is about 9 meters up. Now it lines up with the curved bay's edge, as the print shows one edge wrapping round both.
The side wall is brick, about a third of a meter thick. That is our guess. Neither picture shows it.
The sides and back are a plain pale brick, our guess. The pictures are black and white, so the brick's color can not be read.

Copper gutters run along the roof, with round rain pipes. That is our guess, since neither picture shows a pipe. We moved the north side's pipe a little, so it no longer runs across a basement window.
The windows have two panes over two, with small basement windows. That is our guess. The old drawing is too rough to show the window bars.
Each step is 30 centimeters deep. That is our guess. We can not count the steps in either picture.
The landing at the door is 1.5 meters deep. That is our guess.
The front is brick faced with stone, as in the 1880s. How thick the wall is, is our guess. No picture shows it clearly.
The roof's flat top has a gentle slope, our guess. No picture shows over the roof's bend.

The 1911 map shows a brick home of two floors behind the church, with a small part on the alley. We use its 1911 shape for 1904.
The 1911 map shows a stable for hiring horses. It has a wooden wagon shed and a brick stable, 80 feet long, from Indiana Avenue to the alley. We think it stood in 1904 too.

A history book of 1913 tells us about this church. Its first stone was laid in November 1870. It was finished after October 1871. The last service in it was on 29 December 1912. The 1911 map names it the First Presbyterian Church.

This is the Prairie Avenue front, opening by opening. It comes from a drawing of 1965, and an 1888 photo agrees. Most sizes are measured, to within about half a foot. Over the door is a half circle of wedge-shaped stones.

The street fence comes from a drawing of May 1874 of 1620 next door. It shows a fence of boards along the street, running north past 1620's corner. We read its height off the drawing. It comes out about 1.5 meters.

The 1888 photo shows low square stone posts with solid stone rails between them. There is a gap in line with the steps. That replaces an older guess of a tall iron fence and gates. The heights and shapes are rounded guesses. A thin iron fill in a 1965 photo is from later, so we left it out.

The 1888 picture shows two rows of square holes at the top of the wall. Stone spikes stand at the corners. A deep band of diamond shapes runs below. Five thin columns stand between the six third floor windows. The sizes are rounded readings. The hidden parts are our guess.

A drawing from 1893 shows a balcony with a railing over the door. It sits on the hood above the door. So we built a stone shelf on two brackets, with an iron railing. The drawing does not show what the railing was made of. The iron is our guess.
This sets the base's south-west corner. We placed it from two old photos. One is a print from Detroit. Using both, we moved it a few meters east from where it was.

In the old drawing, the basement windows are tall. They stand almost a floor high at the walk. The front's two outer bays stand behind the curved bay and the wing. So the bay and the wing hold the basement windows.

We read this off the photo. The bay's middle edge, at the second floor, is about 6.3 meters up. The main roof edge is about 9.5 meters up. So the main floor is 4.3 meters tall and the upper one 3.7 meters.

We read the bay's windows off the 1888 picture. The ground floor's run from about 2 to 4.3 meters up. The first floor's run from about 5.5 to 7.6 meters. They are about a meter wide. The third floor's windows are in the gable.

A wide roof window with a peak sits on the front slope. Pictures from 1913 and 1919 show three windows under its peak. We built it 3.3 meters wide, in the middle of the front. The pictures do not agree on just where it stands.
The steps are wide, between side walls. We read them off the 1888 picture. They are about 2.2 meters wide.
This is the building's whole plan, as the old map outlines it. It has the main part with its wall props, and the tower and porch at the 21st Street corner.
This is the church's whole plan, as an old survey drawing shows it. It has the main hall, the parish hall and the north side part. The wall props and the tower's bump are left off.

The front has a bay of one floor with angled sides. We built it from an old photo. It has three faces, each with a pointed window between broad posts. It sits on a panelled base, under a carved edge and a flat top.

The upper floor repeats the group of three windows. It adds a window over the door and a narrow one beside it. We read them off an old drawing. The main floor's narrow window beside the door is laid the same way.

These are our usual window rows, for walls we have no picture of. Every street window is copied from the photo. The main part's side and back walls are blank or hidden. So no window is laid from these.

A stone porch stands at the front's north end. The 1911 map shows it, about 5.5 meters along the front. An old photo shows it is a stone porch of arches, one floor high. Its floor is about 2 meters up. It has a narrow arch and a wide one.

The windows are our usual kind. The picture is too small to count the panes. A photo by Taylor shows a bar across two windows near their tops. So the house's windows are one pane over one, under a small top window.

The windows have two panes over two, our guess. The picture is too small to count the panes. The south side's round-topped windows have one pane over one, under a fan. The basement windows under them have round tops.

The door and its steps come from our door plan. It is a door with four panels under a window of two panes. A dark hall lies behind it. We rebuilt what stands in front of it to match a picture of February 1888. A floor plan printed with that picture helped.

The door and its steps come from our door plan, on straight steps. The front yard is 8.6 meters deep, as the map draws it. The photo shows the steps' open ends between iron rails, with no stone side walls. So we built them that way. The door sits back in the wall, in the dark of the porch.

The door is at the 18th Street end, under the porch. The curved bay's middle is further along. One window over the porch sits above the door. The bay's own windows take the place of the earlier evenly spaced ones. The carved frames are left for later work.

The door sits at the top of straight steps between side walls, as the photo shows. It is under a round arch. A pair of doors sits under a fan-shaped window, set back from the wall. We read its size off the photo.

The door is at the front's north end, beside the shared wall. Our first try put the doors at the pair's outer ends. But the old map puts a stone bay across the south half of 1636's front. So the door goes in the north half. The pair's doors stand together at the shared wall.
The door is at the pair's outer end, the north end of the front. It is beside the side path to 1611. Our rules give it there. 1615's door is at the pair's other outer end.

The door is at the front's south end, beside the shared wall. The old map leaves the front flat there. The angled bay takes the north end. So the pair's doors stand together at the shared wall, with their bays at the outer ends.

The door is at the top of the steps, in the north corner part. The photo and an old picture show it. The steps have solid stone side walls, ending in square posts at the bottom. The door sits deep in a round-arched hole.

The door is in the north strip of the front, beside the curved bay, as the drawing shows. It sits in a round-arched hole. On this side of the street, the plan is turned round. So the end our plan calls south is the north end on the ground.

The door is in the middle bay of the three, as a drawing from 1893 shows. It is a round-topped door at the top of steps, under a balcony. Our first try had put it in the south bay, before any picture was found.

The door is in the front's south bay. The drawing puts the arched doorway, up its steps, south of the arched window. Our plan builds a front as three bays. So the third bay is a narrow blank one at the south corner.

The door's top stays under the porch's top beam, about 4.7 meters up. We read it off a photo from 1898. The door stands in the porch's shadow. It now opens onto a raised floor. So it is as tall as our plan allows, with its top window.
We read the door's sill off an old photo. It is about 1.66 meters above the walk, up eleven steps. A picture of Reid's house shows the steps climbing about as high as Reid's own porch floor.

We say this stood in 1904, and no more. An atlas from 1886 draws the row. The ice cream works only reached the corner after our year. When the corner houses came down is not known.
We say this building stood in 1904, and no more. The 1911 map draws it. When it was built and lost is left for later work.
We say this building stood in 1904, and no more. The 1911 map draws it. When it was built and lost is left for later work.

We say this stood in 1904, and no more. The 1911 map draws it. A museum says the house was finished in 1864 for Granville S. Ingraham. A permit from 1875 for this lot names Henry Strong. The papers do not agree.

The roof edge has carved wooden brackets, as our first try had it, round all four walls. That try gave 1608 brackets so its roof would not copy 1600's. No paper or picture shows it. No iron trim runs along the top. A brick house like this, with a low roof, likely had none.

We say this building stood in 1904, and no more. The 1911 map draws it. The 1886 atlas stops at 18th Street. Nothing else dates it. The end date is just the latest time anything shows it standing. It is not when it was torn down.

We say this building stood in 1904, and no more. The 1911 map draws it. The 1886 atlas stops at 18th Street. Nothing else dates it. The end date is just the latest time anything shows it standing. It is not when it was torn down.

A list says a tall roof floor was added in 1886. The 1911 map gives three floors. The photo shows the house earlier, with two floors under a low roof and a middle gable. So the steep roof is the one from 1886. No picture of it exists. So it is the street's most common kind in 1904, of slate with windows.

A list says the house had tall chimneys. The photo shows a tall brick chimney at the north side, about 2.4 meters behind the front. Its top is about 1.7 meters over the roof's peak. Our model puts it within a tenth of a meter of the photo.

The roof's peak is 3.1 meters behind the front. The back slope falls gently to the back wall. Both shared walls rise above the roof with stone tops. In the photo, 2009's curved gable stands against the north one. Reid's house stands against the south.
We read the roof floor's gable off the drawing. The street wall rises over the curved bay as a steep gable with a peak. Three short windows with gently curved tops sit in it.

A round stair tower stands on the east wing's courtyard side. Its size comes from the old drawings. Its wall top is about 32 feet up, and its pointed roof about 42 feet. A photo from about 1923 shows it in brick, with a pointed roof and a knob on top.

The rough stone base has a cap at 1 meter, over two rows of stone. The drawing shows iron. The steps rise between iron rails, with a post at the top and the bottom. The handrail slopes, and ends in a curl at the foot.
This starts at the same spot as the Wirt Dexter house at 1721. That is its brick block's back corner. It is turned so this part runs toward the house's own front. It runs about 24 meters east.
The window heights come from the 1874 drawing. The upper street windows run from about 7.5 to 9.7 meters up, with round tops. The main floor's tops sit about 6.3 meters up.

We read the second floor's windows off the front photo. A narrow window sits over the door's south side. It is small, about 0.4 by 1.1 meters. Its sill is a little higher than the others on that floor.

The map colors the building brick. The photo shows a stone basement and a stone first floor, with brick floors above. They have stone bands and trim. So the front is stone up to the second floor's band, with brick above. The sides and back are brick.
The map colors the front part brick. A list calls it a brick home of three floors. So we built a brick house, front and all. Every wall is plain brick, with stone trim on the street front.

The map colors the house brick. The old picture shows dark brick walls with light stone trim. The basement, the bands, the window frames and the corner strips are stone. So the walls are brick above a stone basement.
