The map colors the house pink, for brick, over a stone basement. Pictures from 1912, 1913 and 1919 show red pressed brick over a pale stone basement. Pale stone bands run at the floors and windows. So we built that.
The map colors the house pink, for brick. An old Christmas picture shows a brick front in rows. The stone is only the basement and one band under the roof edge.
The map colors the street front blue, for stone, on a pink brick house. A list says brick with a stone front. So the front is stone, with brick side and back walls.

The map draws an open porch of one floor across the north end of the front. It is about 3 meters wide and 2 meters out. Its place and size come from the map. The rest is our guess. It has a board floor, posts with curly brackets, and a ceiling of boards.
The map gives the side walls as 12 inches thick. It gives nothing for the front. So we made the front 12 inches thick too.
The map says two floors and a half. The photo shows three rows of street windows over the basement. The third row is in a low floor, under the roof's slope. That is the map's half floor.

The map says only stone. So the front is our guess, as a house of about 1891 would most likely be. It is rough stone from Lemont, the grey-buff local stone of the time. Its windows have smooth frames. J. Foster Rhodes bought the lot in July 1891 to build on it.

The map shows a back part of two floors behind the main part. It sticks out past the south side, with a short front of its own. An old photo shows it as a lower block under a low roof on brackets, beside the house.
The map shows a brick back part behind the main part, two floors under a flat tin top. No picture shows it. So its windows and heights are our guess. We lowered its floors with the main part's.

The map draws an angled stone bay on the front, near the south corner. It is about 3.8 meters across and almost a meter out. We built it with our angled bay plan. It rises three floors, in the front's brownstone.
The map draws an angled stone bay at the north end of the front. It mirrors 1636's. The map draws the pair with a bay at each outer end. We built it with our angled bay plan.
The map's colors say stone. The photo shows the front and the 18th Street side both in cut stone. So it is an all-stone house.

The map shows the main part behind the front part. It is 8.4 meters wide and runs back to its back wall. It has a part of three floors and a back part of two. Two pictures show its south side in brick.
The map shows a block at the north-west corner and a tall part on the 18th Street side. Both rise the full height, as the photo shows. We built them sticking out as far as our plan allows.
These are the map's boxes that the house itself does not carry. They make up the stable. We once added a part past its east wall, from a photo. Now we do not.

The map shows a shallow tall part on the front, about 5.5 meters wide. It rises the full height, with three windows on each floor. A wide window sits between two narrow ones. It rises past the main roof edge to its own top, as the Doane photo shows.
The map shows a stone part at the north end of the front. It is the porch the photo shows there, behind a street tree. It has columns holding a balcony with a railing, at the second floor.

The map shows two boxes behind the main part. The photo shows their walls and roofs on the 18th Street side. One is a gabled part. Its side runs straight with the 18th Street wall, as the map and the photo show.

The map shows a brick back part of two floors behind the house. A newspaper of 1869 says the kitchen was 13 feet tall and the floor above it 12 feet. It says the back part was 37 feet high to the top of its roof edge. So we built it to that height.
The map shows a wooden bay of two floors on the Prairie front. So its place, floors and wood come from the map. Its shape is our plan's. It is about 2 meters out, across the south part of the front.

The photo shows the north wall's window at too steep an angle to measure. So we used our usual windows, shorter on the low third floor. They are as short as our plan allows, so they fit under the roof edge.
The side and back walls are not in the picture. They are the street's plain brick, as photos from 2003 show.
The side steps are about 1.2 meters wide. A small floor plan from an old magazine shows that. The plan is too rough to read it closer than about a fifth of a meter.
A photo shows a steep slate roof with a nearly straight face. A roof window sits over the porch. Iron trim runs along its top edge. We read it off the photo.

The steep slate roof rises 4.5 meters over the top of the wall. That is the most our plan allows. An old drawing puts the bend about 15 meters up. A picture from 1883 agrees. Iron trim, about half a meter high, runs round the top.

The steep slate roof rises about 4.5 meters over the top of the wall. A photo from 1898 shows it. Its faces are steep and nearly straight. Three roof windows with small peaks stand over the three columns of windows.

The front photo shows the steep slate roof's bend about 12.4 meters up. Iron trim runs along it. A roof window with a peak sits on the front, and another on the south side. The tall front part has its own steep roof.
The map draws a small wooden piece on 1615's south wall, in the path toward 1619. It is about 1.6 meters long and half a meter out. No list names it. 1613 has nothing on its path wall.

The south bay has angled sides. It stands on the ground at the south end of the front, under its own bracketed roof edge. A low cap with iron trim tops it. Both old pictures show three round-topped windows on each floor.

This is the south end of the house's front wall. We read it off the 1911 map, where the front and south wall lines meet. That map lines up with the ground to about 3 meters. The front stands about 11 meters back from Prairie Avenue.
This is the south side. We read it off a photo, fitted to Hunt's floor plan. A column of windows stands just behind the angled corner, about 3 meters back.
The south side has no windows. A photo from about 1870 shows it blank brick from the front corner to the angled bay. Nothing says the later rebuild opened it.

A glass house sits on the south side. The 1911 map shows a bulge there and writes 'Greenhouse'. An old picture shows a curved glass house on a stone base, with a balcony over it. We built it as a curved bay, 8.4 meters across and 2.7 meters out.
The south side's front column of windows is about 5.8 meters behind the front. We read it off a photo. The windows behind it are on the side bay.

This is the south side's front column of windows. It sits between the south bay and the porch. The old drawing shows two round-topped windows on each floor. They sit behind the porch's columns and over its balcony.

This is the south tall part on the front. The 1911 map shows it sticking out about a meter. It is about 5.7 meters wide, in the front's stone. It has one broad window on each floor and two barred basement windows. We read them off an old drawing.
The photo shows the south part of the front sticking out. It runs up through the basement and two floors to a flat top at the third floor. The balcony stands on that top. It is about 5 meters across.
We read the south wall's windows off the photo. Over the lower south part are a single round-topped window and a pair. Toward the back is another pair on both floors.

This is the south wall, toward 1811. A photo from 1965 shows one column of windows near the corner. A tree hides the rest of the wall. Past the bay, the photo shows no window. So we took out the two we had guessed.
This is the south-west corner of the house. We moved it toward the street and south, onto the back corner of the wide front part. So the narrow back part becomes a back wing behind it.
This is the south-west corner of the house, on the wall shared with 1636. We read that shared line again for the pair, and moved the corner to it.

This is the stable's granite wall on the alley. We read its openings as gaps on the old plans. No drawing shows their heights. The upper opening belongs to the roof window that sticks out. We now size the openings by the rule of the rest.
This is the stable's south block, as the 1911 map draws it. It runs from its west wall to its east wall, and to its front on 18th Street. We made its angled corner square.

No drawing or photo shows the stable's south end. An old plan draws its south wall in brick. A plain brick gable, like the north end's roof, is the simplest guess. A roof of four slopes is just as likely.
This is the base's box. The plinth, the stone block, the cap and the figures stand on its middle.
We read the steps off the photo. They are about 2 meters wide, between their side walls.
Both photos show the steep roof's faces straight, with level rows of slate. They lean at 72 degrees. They rise 2 meters from the top of the side walls to the bend.

The stone basement's top is about 2 meters above the ground. We read it off the photo. Its round-topped windows show over the fence. So the main floor is there. This guess is good to about a third of a meter.
We read the stone main part off the 1911 map. It is about 22 meters deep and 15 meters across. The map's porch, side bays and brick back part stand on it.
Both photos show a stone porch on columns over the steps. Its flat top is a balcony with a railing. It is about 4.4 meters wide. The 1911 map shows a stone box the same width.

The street wall is stone in neat rows. It is rough stone from Lemont. A base of two rows sits under a cap. Corner stones run long and short. Two stone bands cross it. A flat arch of wedge-shaped stones sits over each opening.
The roof is flat, behind the roof edge, as our rules drew it for stone-front houses. A tin top falls to the back wall. Low walls with stone caps run on each side. No paper or picture shows this roof.
The steps run between the porch's pairs of columns. They are about 2.6 meters wide. We read them off a photo from 1898.
A drawing from 1893 shows two rails on the steps. Their pattern is our guess. The rough base's top is our guess too.

The front's carved trim comes from our trim plan. The main floor's windows get a frame with a small roof on curly brackets. A carved panel of leaves sits below. The second floor gets only the small roof. The third floor keeps plain stone tops. So the trim gets lighter going up.
A drawing from 1893 shows the front's windows with round tops. The main floor's outer bays have pairs of them. Each upstairs bay has one. The basement windows come in pairs under the outer bays.

The front windows have a stone top under a small roof, on both floors. That was the plainest and most common kind on a brick front of the 1870s on Prairie Avenue. The door keeps a flat stone top. No paper or picture shows 1608's window tops.

We read the front windows off the 1874 drawing. The upper windows over the bay and over the door both have round tops. Each sits under a heavy round hood.

The street line comes from the 1904 street map. One big lot held 2000, 2010 and 2018. This house's share runs halfway to each neighbor. No picture shows the front. So we left it open, like the houses across the street at 2001 to 2005.

The street windows are the kinds the photo shows. The lower floors have windows that open like doors, split by posts. A window of four panes sits over the door. The second floor's have gently curved tops. The side and back walls are not in the photo.

A tall chimney stands on the north side. We read it off an old drawing. It is about 17.5 meters high. It stands on the roof edge over the north wall. The iron trim on top leaves no room for it there.
This is the back part, behind the main part. It is about 10.6 meters deep. It has three floors, as the map says. Its windows and flat top are our guess.
This is the back wing's south-west corner. It sits 2 meters behind where our first try put it. The house runs from the wing's back wall to the stone front.

These are the middles of the two bays along the front, read off the photo. One holds the bump and the big arched window over it. The other holds the door, a pair of windows, and a small arched window. We moved the door to the middle of the porch arch.
In Taylor's print, the two windows over the porch each sit in a carved frame. Each has a small roof over it. So the second floor wears our plain carved frames.

A picture from 1913 shows two tall chimneys rising off the north side, well above the roof. One is between the round tower and the angled corner. One is further back. Their height over the roof is our guess.

We read the upper street windows off the 1874 drawing. The window over the door sits a little south of the door's middle. It is behind a tree. Before, we had it right over the door.
The porch's floor is at the main floor. Its front edge is about 1.85 meters above the ground, from an old photo. The basement windows show under it.

The old picture shows an iron fence either side of the walk. It has big S-shaped curls between posts with balls on top. It has no spikes. So we built a fence of S-shaped curls, every other one flipped.

The old picture shows a porch at the top of the steps. Columns stand before the door, under a round arch. A railing sits on top. A drawing from about 1914 shows a wide entrance, about 4.9 meters across. So we built a stone porch on columns, with a stone railing.
In the old picture, the steps are wide, almost as wide as the porch. So they are 4.8 meters wide. The porch's columns stand at the two ends of the landing.

An old photo from before 1880 shows a deep roof edge on pairs of brackets. It runs round the main part and the lower part. Photos from about 1897 to 1906 show the same on the south side. So the new front of 1880 left the roof edge as it was.
A walk of flat stones runs from the steps through the railing's gap to the sidewalk. A cinder path runs from the side gate back along the south lot line. The stones, width and wear are our guesses.

The walls are painted over the brick. The photo shows them almost as light as the sky, against the dark windows. The photo is black and white. So we know how light they were, but not their color. A pale stone color is our guess.

The walls are painted over the brick. A newspaper of 1887 called the house roomy and olive green. A brick house of 1872 that was olive green must have been painted. That was the fashion of the 1870s. The 1874 drawing shows the front smooth, with no brick rows.
We read the top of the walls off the 1874 drawing again. The roof edge's bottom is about 10.6 meters up at both corners. Its top is about 10.9 meters up. So the top of the wall is at 10.9 meters.
The top of the stone basement is about 2.2 meters above the ground. We read it off the photo. The door's sill sits on it.

The stone band under the main floor is about 2.4 meters above the walk. A drawing from about 1914 shows it. We built it at 2.5 meters. A picture from 1898 shows a long straight flight of about fourteen steps. That agrees with this height.

The whole house comes from our wooden house plan. It is one half of a pair. An atlas from 1886 gives its size, 10.5 meters deep and 4.75 meters along Prairie. Neither half builds the wall between them. So the pair stands as one wooden block with one long front.

The whole house comes from our wooden house plan. It is one half of a pair. An atlas from 1886 gives its size, 10.5 meters deep and 5.25 meters along Prairie. Neither half builds the wall between them. So the pair stands as one wooden block with one long front.

The width comes from the map. We read the gable's openings off the photo. Its twin windows are two pointed ones.
The 1911 map draws three bays. The front's angled bay sits near the south corner, about 1.25 meters out. A photo from about 1897 shows it rising through the basement and both floors.

There are three bays across the front. The north bay is the entrance. It sits in the middle of the open porch, as the 1888 picture shows. So the door and the window over the balcony are in its middle.
There are three bays across the 10.65 meter front. The main floor has a pair of windows, the door, and another pair. Upstairs there is one window in each bay. A drawing from 1893 shows them.
There are three bays along the front. The north bay is behind the stone corner porch. The entrance is in the middle. The bay of two floors is at the south end.
There are three bays, read off the photo. The south bay's windows are in its middle. The entrance and the window over it are in the front's middle. The north bay mirrors the south one.

There are three columns of openings on the front, north of the corner bay. The door and a pair of windows over the porch are one. Two more stand further along. The upper windows sit over the main floor's.

Three small roof windows with pointed roofs and knobs stand on the east wing's courtyard slope. Each has one square pane. The old drawing gives their size and place. A photo from about 1923 shows them. There are none on the Prairie slope.
Three chimneys stand where the old drawing shows them. Two are on the north wall, one near the front and one near the back. The third is on the south wall. Both pictures show that one.

Three windows on each floor run along one side wall. They look over the narrow path between 1613 and 1611. There is one for each room of a house three rooms deep. The other side wall is shared with 1615, so it is blank.
Three windows on each floor run along the north wall, one for each room. The house has the same on its south side, like 1628. The wall faces the side yard toward 1620, so it gets windows.
Three windows on each floor run along the south wall, one for each room. The wall faces the side yard of 1638, the Shortall-Gregory cottage.
Three windows on each floor sit in the back wall. A small part on the map joins the south part of this wall. When it is built, one window becomes the door into it.

We read the Prairie front off the photo, from the north wall. The door's bay is between bands of rough stone. A tall window is in the middle bay. Another is in the south bay. The owner of this project looked at it too.

We read the roof off the photo. Its steep straight sides rise from the roof edge, about 12 meters up, to the bend at about 16.8 meters. Iron trim almost a meter high runs round the top. Four roof windows with round tops stand on it.
We read this off the photo. The steep straight roof rises from the roof edge to its bend, about 15.7 meters up. Two roof windows stand on the front.
We read the windows off the photo. The main ones are about 0.9 meters wide, from about 2.5 to 5.4 meters up. The upper ones are about the same width, from about 7 to 9.2 meters up.
There are twelve steps, each 28 centimeters deep, with a landing. The flight stops just short of the street line. It is a rounded guess from the old picture.
The 1911 map draws two bays here. So their places come from the map. Their shape is our plan's. On the front is an angled bay on the south half. On the south wall is a small bump.
This house has two bays. A list names a curved bay at the south end, from an 1888 picture. That picture is not one of our sources. So its size and windows are our guess.

Two tall stone chimneys stand on the south side. One is near the front corner. The other is beside the roof window over the angled bay. They rise above the roof's bend, in the walls' pale stone.

We read the Prairie front's windows off an old print from Detroit. The second floor has three round-arched windows between bands of rough stone. One is over the porch.

The steps are as wide as the porch behind the arch, 2.3 meters. Their side walls stand at the arch's posts. We read them off the photo. The rest is our guess.

The house is weathered to its own age on 1 July 1904, on all its brick and stone. It was the block's newer house. A build date of 1901 is a limit, not a sure date. An atlas from 1886 shows a different house on the lot.

The photo shows the south wall as blank brick on both floors, except for the bay window. It has no window and no stone band. So we took out the five windows we had guessed there.

The photo shows the basement in smooth light stone, up to a stone band at the main floor. That is about 2 meters up. Brick is above it, on the front, the bay and the south side. A list says stone basement and bands.

The photo shows the basement in smooth pale stone, in rows about a third of a meter high. A stone band at the main floor is about 2 meters up. The brick stands on it. So we built smooth stone to there.
In the photo, the entrance is a tall dark round arch in the front's middle bay. It is between the corner porch and the stone bay. Its top is about 5.8 meters up.
In the photo, the steps start at the arch. The porch's floor is the landing. The side walls run level a short way, then sweep down. We read this off the photo. The rest is our guess.
The photo shows a low pale wall along the street line. We read it off the photo. Its top is about three quarters of a meter high.
In the photo, the south wall's roof edge is plain, with almost no overhang. So we made it tiny. The photo shows no gutter across the front.

The photo shows a tall light stone column on the front's south corner. It runs from the stone basement's top to a carved top under the roof edge. It is almost half a meter wide on each face. We wrapped it round both faces.
The 1911 map draws a piece behind the north end of the back wall. A list calls it a brick piece of two floors. Its place and floors come from the map. Its shape is our guess.
The 1911 map draws a piece behind the north part of the back wall. A list calls it a brick piece of one floor over a basement. Its place and floors come from the map. Its shape is our guess.
The 1911 map draws pieces behind the front block. Their places and floors come from the map. Their shapes are our guess. One is a brick back wing of two floors over a basement.
The plan now comes from the 1911 map, not our rules. It has a part of two floors and a stable of one and a half floors. Both lean a little, as the map draws them.

The old picture shows three iron balconies on the front. One is in front of the north upper window. One is over the door. One is in front of the wide window. Each stands on two curly stone brackets, at the upper floor.

The old picture, photos from the 1950s and 1967, and the owner's photo all show a flat top. No roof slope or window shows over the wall. So the roof is flat, behind low walls. What covered it, nobody knows.
The pictures show pale stone bands across the front part's brick. A picture from 1919 shows them along the north side's back parts too. So the bands run round at the same lines.
A picture from 1919 shows the pale basement going round the north side, under the brick. We made the south side match.
The window frames look white in all three pictures, like the porch columns. So they are painted white, not dark green.

The map and all three pictures show a pale stone basement under the brick. The pictures show pale bands across the brick at each floor. So we built smooth stone from Lemont up to the main floor, with brick above.
The map shows the steps, about 2.6 by 3.4 meters. The Detroit print shows them rising between the porch's columns. The porch floor carries on either side. The steps now rise in line with the door.
The side and back walls, and their chimneys, are the same red-brown brick as the front. They are not the street's pale brick. The photo shows both chimneys as dark as the front's brick.
The stair beside the porch is 2 meters wide. The old plan shows a little more. We made it a bit smaller, so it clears the curved bay. The plan is a small print, so this is our guess.
The stone band under the low top wall sticks out a third of a meter. The old picture shows a thin carved band over the diamond band, not a deep roof edge.
In the photo, the steps run between the porch's columns. Their south ends step down beside a column's base. They are 1.7 meters wide, clear of both bases.
In the photo, the top step stands just in front of the porch's columns. The landing runs back under the porch.
The front's brick is a red-brown. The side and back walls stay a plain pale brick. Levy's print shows the front's brick much darker than its stone. A photo from about 1955 shows the south wall paler.
The third floor runs flat across the whole front, over the curved bay. It is one row of six windows, split by thin columns. The old picture and photos from the 1950s and 1967 show it.
The two south chimneys stand in the south wall's gable. The 1888 picture and an old print both show them. The tall one rises from the gable's front slope, a little behind the front.
We read the upper floor's three street windows off the photo. Each has a gently curved top. A flat carved hood sits over each one.
The walls are brick, as the map shows. Two pictures from 1887 and 1912 show it darker than the slate spire. That means a red brick.
The stone band under the main floor is about 2 meters above the walk. We read it off a photo fitted to Hunt's floor plan. An 1893 picture had given a bit more.
The 1911 map draws a wing behind the back wall. A list calls it a brick back wing of two floors, with a part of one floor at its end. Its place and floors come from the map. Its shape is our guess.

In the photo, a round-topped doorway is about 1.4 meters wide. Its top is about 3.3 meters over the landing. A stone hood and a middle stone sit over it. The doors are in shadow. The steps have no stone side walls.

These faces use the courtyard's slightly pink brick, with grey mortar. The brick size is the same as the walls already have. The joints are drawn on, not built. Their depth and color changes are our guesses.

We read where the chimneys stand off the floor plan printed with the 1888 picture. It shows two fireplaces in the main part, each set across a corner. One is the library's. One is the hall's, at the foot of the stair.

The 1911 map draws the house three floors high, all the way back to the coach house. So the part behind the front has three floors under a tin top. The map colors it stone. It is built as a brick wing. Later work made the back part about 32 feet wide, so its south wall runs back in line with the front's, as the photos show. The map's wider house is the house after it was changed. No picture shows the back part, so this is our guess.

The front part of the house, from the outline on the 1911 map. It is about 57 feet deep. A part for the stairs on the north side, a corner bay, a slanted side bay and a back wing are added onto it. Later work built the front about 32 feet wide, not the map's 34. Both photos show the corner bay's south face about two and a half feet past the main front's south wall. So the main wall stands that far inside the bay. The 1911 map shows the house after it was changed, with no corner bay. A 1904 front built to the photos does not use it.

The 1911 map draws this house. So it was there in 1904. The photo shows the same plan, with the round north-west corner and the part that sticks out on the south side. We do not know when the photo was taken.

The 1911 map draws more parts behind the front of the house. The list of the street's houses names a wide side wing with its own pointed roof. It sticks out about 14 feet from the south side. It starts about 26 feet behind the front and is about 17 feet long. The photo shows it. It has one window on each floor in its west side. Its roof edge is about 36 feet up. Its pointed slate roof faces south and rises to about 48 feet. Behind it is a part with two floors under a slate roof. Behind that are two back parts. One has two floors and one has one floor. Both have flat roofs. No picture shows them. So their floors, roofs and windows are guesses.

We read these heights off the photo. A stripe of brick runs under the second-floor windows, about 19 feet up. The second-floor windows are from about 20 to 28 feet up. The roof edge on the south side is about 32 feet up.
The basement has windows under the big front window and under the narrow side window. In the photo they are dark openings. They are about 1 to 4 feet over the snow.

The old 1911 map shows where the back of the front part of the house ends. The map was matched to known street crossings. That makes it close, but it was not checked another way. It could be off by less than a foot. An earlier guess put this corner about 34 feet further back and about 4 feet south. It had left out a strip on the north side.

The top of the front's pointed roof is about 51 feet over the ground. The roof edge below it is about 32 feet up. The front is about 30 feet wide. So the pointed front is steep. The roof behind it is a little less steep. The top of the front wall stands about a foot over the roof's peak.

The front windows are read off the photo. On the main floor they run from about 8 to 16 feet up. They are about 4 feet wide. On the second floor they run from about 20 to 28 feet up. They are a bit narrower.

In the photo, the main roof runs back from the street under one peak. You can see its whole south slope, from the front's pointed wall to the tall chimney. The street end of the roof hides behind the pointed front. So the two long slopes match the photo.
In the photo, the porch floor and the bottom stripe of the front are at the same height. That is about 7 feet over the yard. The steps climb to it in about eleven steps.
The porch door sits under a round arch in the brick front. The photo shows the arch. Every street window has a square top. So no other window is round on top.

A list of the street's houses names a round-arched porch. The photo shows a wide round arch. Its top is about 16 feet over the ground. It is about 6 feet wide. Inside it is a porch with a small window in its north wall. The door is at its south end. Here the arch holds the door, set into the brick front. The deep porch, its small window and its south door are left out.
The second-floor windows are read off the photo. One is beside the tower. A wide one sits over the main floor's wide window. Over the porch, the tower fills that floor.
The south side has one narrow window on each floor. It is about 5 feet behind the front corner. In the photo the rest of that side is blank, up to the wing.

A list of the street's houses names a steep pointed front. The front wall goes up across its whole width to a point about 51 feet up. Its sloping edges are straight. Three attic windows sit high in it, from about 32 to 38 feet up. Each is about 2 feet wide, and the left two are a pair. In the photo the slate runs a little past the sloping edges. Here a stone cap covers the edge instead.
The front has two rows of openings, read off the photo. One is the porch's round arch, under the tower at the north end. The other is the wide windows of both floors.

The photo shows three chimneys. Two of them stand here. The tall one is on the south side, about 16 feet behind the front. Its top is about 54 feet up. The other is over the north wall, behind the tower. The third stands on the roof about 36 feet back, over a back part. It is left out.

Every outside wall above the basement was faced with the best pressed brick from Baltimore, the 1869 newspaper said. In 1898 it called the house "his big red brick house." Now every wall is smooth, even red brick. Before, a rough red-brown brick stood in. It looked too much like the stone, so it all looked like one red lump. The exact shade of red is our guess.

In 1869 a paper said the base was brownstone, rubbed smooth, with deep lines between the blocks. It was 6 feet high, under the brick. The photo shows the pale stone base under the dark brick. Now all the trim is brownstone too. That means the sills, the tops of the windows, the bands and the porch. Before, it was pale cream stone. The carved parts and the front steps are brownstone too. The base on the front has three deep lines cut in it.

The brown stone runs around the side walls up to the main floor, the newspaper said. The photo shows it along the south side. Now the stone is cut in blocks, as the paper said. There is a thick stone at the bottom. Above it are four rows of stone with deep lines between them. A stone ledge sits on top. The tower and the side bays have the same base. The number of rows and their sizes are our guess.
This is the plain brick inside the walls. The red pressed brick is laid over it on every wall. The 1869 newspaper said all the outside walls were pressed brick.

We read the plan off the 1911 map and the rooms in the 1869 newspaper. A square tower stands on the front, 3.8 meters across. It rises past the roof edge to a lookout on top. We built it square, as the photo shows. Now the tower is red brick on a brownstone base, like the walls. The bay on the south side is brownstone, as the newspaper said.
